tasks.short: Assess the emergency on site, call police or fire, direct guards and evacuation, and log the call and times.

steps.what: Security supervisor assesses the emergency such as fire, bomb threat or unauthorized persons
Security supervisor calls police or fire departments
Security supervisor directs guards and evacuation
Security supervisor logs the emergency call and times in the logbook

tasks.design: The incident form in the security system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) takes alarm times and the time of the emergency call from the alarm and phone systems, so the supervisor adds only what happened instead of reconstructing times in a logbook. Assessing the emergency, calling the services and directing people stay with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Times were reconstructed from memory and written in a logbook.
tasks.enabler_now: Alarm and phone systems record event times that forms can import.
tasks.still_hard: In a real emergency nobody fills forms until it is over.
tasks.human_edge: Deciding in seconds whether to evacuate.

reach.learn: Whether event times are accurate afterwards.

evidence.claim: Alarm and phone systems record event times that incident forms can import.

assumptions: Boundary: from the emergency to the emergency logged; the services' response is outside.
Input contract: alarm and phone systems connected; fallback is the logbook.
Assessing and calling do not change.
Emergency services' time does not change.
research_questions: Are incident times accurate in evaluations?

incremental.description: Security supervisor corrects imported times when systems disagree.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: short emergencies; high: long incidents with many events.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch camera feeds, judge what is seen and act, search recordings after incidents, and log observations.

steps.what: Security supervisor monitors closed-circuit television cameras
Security supervisor judges what is seen and acts
Security supervisor searches recordings after incidents

tasks.design: The video system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) raises an alert when motion is detected in set zones during set hours (fences, loading docks at night), so the supervisor does not watch every feed equally. Alarm events bookmark the footage, so recordings are found from the event list instead of scrolling. Observations are logged on the event. Judging what is seen and acting stay with the supervisor. No behaviour or face analysis is used.
tasks.previous_blocker: All feeds were watched equally and recordings scrolled by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Video systems detect motion in zones and bookmark footage at alarm events.
tasks.still_hard: Animals and weather trigger zone alerts.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a person at the fence is lost, not breaking in.
tasks.altitude: The supervisor attends to alerts first.

reach.learn: Whether footage is handed over sooner.

evidence.claim: Video systems can detect motion in set zones and hours and bookmark footage at alarm events.
A DPIA is mandatory for systematic monitoring of employees.

assumptions: Boundary: from camera feeds to observations logged; police investigation is outside.
Input contract: zones and hours set per site; fallback is watching all feeds.
Judging and acting stay with the supervisor.
Cameras are not used to check staff without works council consent.
research_questions: How many zone alerts are false?

incremental.description: Security supervisor dismisses false zone alerts.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: busy sites with many false alerts; high: quiet sites at night.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Plan training and track certificates, teach procedures, first aid and fire safety, test knowledge, coach staff on the job, and record training done.

steps.what: Security supervisor plans training and tracks certificates in a spreadsheet
Security supervisor trains security personnel on protective procedures, first aid and fire safety
Security supervisor tests knowledge with paper quizzes
Security supervisor coaches staff on the job
Security supervisor records training done on paper

tasks.design: Certificates for first aid, fire safety and security licences are held in the learning system ({LMS}) with expiry dates, which reminds staff and the supervisor before they lapse. Knowledge tests run as online quizzes scored by code. Training done is ticked in the same system. Teaching, drills and on-the-job coaching stay with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Certificates were tracked in spreadsheets and quizzes marked by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning systems track expiry dates and score quizzes.
tasks.still_hard: Practical skills need drills, not quizzes.
tasks.human_edge: Running a fire drill that staff take seriously.

evidence.claim: Learning systems can track certificate expiry dates and score quizzes.

assumptions: Boundary: from training needs to training recorded; external certification exams are outside.
Input contract: certificates loaded once; fallback is the spreadsheet.
Teaching and coaching do not change.
Guards take quizzes in about the time paper took.

incremental.description: Security supervisor keeps quiz questions current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small team; high: many guards with many certificates.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Explain policies in briefings, answer staff questions on procedures, write memos on rule changes, check them, and send them to staff.

steps.what: Security supervisor explains company policies and procedures to staff in briefings
Security supervisor answers staff questions on procedures by phone and e-mail
Security supervisor writes memos on rule changes
Security supervisor checks the final memo
Security supervisor e-mails the memo to staff

tasks.design: The current procedures sit in a searchable handbook on the guards' phones ({DOCS}), with each procedure versioned, so routine questions are answered there instead of by e-mail. Rule changes are written as a change to the handbook with a short memo template; once checked, the memo goes to staff from the handbook and shows on their phones. Briefings stay with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Procedures were in binders and changes sent as loose e-mails.
tasks.enabler_now: Versioned handbooks on phones with change notices are easy to run.
tasks.still_hard: Guards on remote sites read little between shifts.
tasks.human_edge: Explaining why a rule matters with a real incident.

reach.learn: Whether questions about routine rules fall.

evidence.claim: Versioned handbooks on phones with change notices are easy to run.
Working and rest-time rules need works council consent under WOR article 27(1)(b).

assumptions: Boundary: from the policy set to the memo sent; policy decisions are outside.
Input contract: handbook kept by the supervisor; fallback is binders and e-mail.
Guards look things up in about the time an e-mail took.

incremental.description: Security supervisor keeps the handbook current.

approvals.approved_version: The memo as checked by the supervisor in s4.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few written changes; high: many questions and rule changes.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The security supervisor keeps handling emergencies, judging camera events, training and briefing staff; logbooks, feed watching and certificate spreadsheets shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A supervisor with more time coaching guards.
